transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Martin Keller (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood CSM); James Patel (Verdant CTO), Elena Ruiz (Verdant Head of Infra), Marcus Lee (Verdant Security Architect), Samantha Ortiz (Verdant Compliance)

Summary:
Quick architecture deep dive focused on Private/VPC deployment options, network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, KMS/HSM integration, audit logs and SOC2/ISO evidentiary questions. Customer is evaluating Private (VPC) vs on-prem air-gapped for regulated accounts; they want specifics for ingress patterns, egress controls, and audit log retention.

Topics covered:
- Private deployment topology (control plane vs data plane)
- VPC peering, PrivateLink equivalents, and peered connectivity patterns
- Ingress: ALB, NAT, internal load balancers, bastion/jump hosts, forward proxies
- Egress control: NAT gateways, egress filtering, proxying, allowlists
- Firewalling and network ACL recommendations (cloud and on-prem)
- KMS / HSM and customer-managed keys (CMK)
- Audit logs, SIEM forwarding, retention, and tamper-evidence
- Compliance artifacts: SOC2, ISO27001, penetration tests

[00:00] Martin Keller (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining; we'll do a deep dive on the private/vpc architecture today, focus on ingress/egress and the security controls. Priya and I will run through the common patterns and then Marcus we wanted to hear yor current constraints, so over to you

[00:18] James Patel (Verdant): yeah, thanks. main ask i guess is we have regulated customers and we need to underdstand where data resides, what touches it, encryption keys, and egress flows, like what leaves our network. we're leaning private vpc but may need an on-prem air gap for some lines of business.

[00:34] Priya Singh (Redwood): cool; quick note first - when we say Private deployment with Redwood we normally mean customer-controlled VPC for the data plane, and optional private control plane depending on contract. data plane sits in your VPC, you provide subnets and SGs. control plane can be in our managed infra with private peering, or fully customer-hosted in on-prem options.

[00:52] Marcus Lee (Verdant): can you clarify control plane traffic? does it need to hit the public internet, or is it all over private peering?

[01:05] Priya: good question. we offer both. for VPC Private we have a private control plane option which uses VPC peering or PrivateLink-style endpoints to talk to the control plane so there is no internet egress for control messages. if you require total isolation we have an on-prem packet for the control plane where everything is customer-hosted (note: some customers call that air-gap but really it's a customer-managed control plane).

[01:30] Elena Ruiz (Verdant): about ingress: we currently run ALBs in front of our internal services and we use a forward proxy for egress filtering. for Redwood's private node workers, do you expect us to terminate TLS at our load balancer or at the Redwood runtime?

[01:48] Priya: two common patterns: TLS termination at your ALB and mTLS onward to the worker, or pass-through TLS to the worker pods. recommended is TLS termination at the ALB with mutual-TLS or client certs to the workers; we also support customer-managed certs and can integrate with ACM or on-prem cert stores. we'll share sample ALB configs.

[02:05] Marcus: ok and for firewall rules, do you provide a list of IP ranges that need to be allowed for the control plane? we have strict allowlists.

[02:17] Martin: yes, we publish a set of control plane CIDR ranges per region and per environment. for the Private offering we also support VPC peering so you don't need public allowlists; otherwise you can restrict to our egress IP pool. note that those IP ranges may change with deployments so we recommend using PrivateLink/peering when possible.

[02:38] Samantha Ortiz (Verdant): audit question - how do we get audit logs for model access and admin actions? we need logs forwarded to our SIEM with tamper evidence for audits.

[02:50] Priya: our Private offering writes detailed audit logs locally in your VPC - admin events, token usage, model version rollouts, who accessed which request id. we support Kafka/SQS/S3 sinks and can forward CloudTrail-like events to your SIEM. timestamps: we include metadata for tamper-evidence and sign-in events. for hosted control plane we provide an immutable log export; for customer-hosted control plane you control log storage and retention.

[03:23] James: retention length - we generally need 7 years for certain data; can Redwood support long-term cold storage?

[03:31] Priya: yes, you can configure log sinks to S3 with lifecycle rules and Glacier for cold storage. audit logs from the data plane can be exported to S3 with encryption using your CMK.

[03:46] Marcus: on the KMS side - is it customer-managed keys only or do you offer HSM integration? our policy requires HSM-backed keys for production L3 data.

[03:58] Priya: we support AWS KMS customer-managed CMKs, and we have integrations for HSMs via external key managers (XKM) - e.g., CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM, and external HSMs via KMIP for on-prem. for full key custody we recommend a CMK with key policy restricted to your account; Redwood services can be granted decryption via IAM or key grants depending on the deployment model. for air-gapped on-prem we support local HSMs.

[04:27] Elena: great. network egress - we want to force egress through our corporate proxy and block direct internet for workers. how do you handle that?

[04:36] Priya: you can route workers through a NAT/proxy in your VPC. two approaches: 1) classsic NAT + proxy with egress allowlist so workers only talk to your proxy and the control plane endpoints; 2) route table with no default route to internet and only specific endpoints reachable via PrivateLink or VPC peering. we also support explicit egress filtering with network policies on pods.

[05:05] Marcus: do you support iptables-level rules or do we need to rely solely on security groups and NACLs?

[05:12] Priya: both - at the cloud level we recommend SGs + NACLs for coarse control. within the nodes we can run host-level iptables/nftables via a bootstrap config. we also provide recommended iptables snippets and sample Calico policies for pod-level filtering.

[05:28] James: what about outbound DNS? we want to prevent DNS exfiltration.

[05:33] Priya: lock down DNS to your resolver, use RFC 6762 policies and explicit allow for DNS requests. we recommend using a DNS forwarder that logs queries and sending those logs to your SIEM. for added security you can run a DNS proxy inside the VPC.

[05:48] Martin: small note - sometimes in our docs KV cache gets transcribed as KV cash, ignore that :)

[05:55] Elena: on firewalling appliances - we run Palo Alto and Transit VPCs; how would the private nodes sit behind the transit?

[06:05] Priya: typical pattern is workers in private subnets with no IGW. egress flows go through a transit gateway that forces traffic through your firewall cluster (Palo Alto/Checkpoint) and then to a NAT or egress proxy. we can place interface endpoints for S3 or other services in those subnets. if you use a transit VPC, we recommend internal ALBs/front doors in front of the workers and stick to private IP access.

[06:30] Marcus: curious about RBAC / SSO. our policy requires SAML SSO + SCIM provisioning and role-based least privilege. how do we integrate?

[06:41] Martin: we support SAML 2.0 SSO and SCIM for user provisioning, and RBAC with fine-grained roles: admin, devops, app, read-only, etc. you can map your groups to Redwood roles. for private installs the control plane honors your IDP for admin auth and you can audit those auth events.

[06:58] Samantha: for SOC2 evidence we'll need change logs and admin approvals. does Redwood produce artifact packages for audits?

[07:06] Liam: yes, we provide an audit bundle for SOC2 reviews containing configuration snapshots, admin user lists, rotation records, key management evidence, and sample logs. we'll share the exact list with you.

[07:20] James: slightly concerned about model caching - i see mention of KV cache. does that persist any customer PII? we want to ensure no sensitive payload is stored on disk unencrypted.

[07:32] Priya: KV cache is only for model attention caching and not intended to persist user PII. we always recommend application-layer filtering to avoid sending PII to models where possible. where caching is enabled we encrypt cache using your CMK at rest and we can disable persistent cache entirely if you require ephemeral only.

[07:55] Marcus: logging format - do logs include request payloads by default? our policy says payloads must be redacted unless explicitly allowed.

[08:05] Priya: payload logging is configurable. by default we log metadata and request ids; payload logging is disabled unless explicitly enabled and then we provide redaction hooks. you'll get headers, token usage and latency metrics by default.

[08:18] Elena: what about performance overhead for mTLS and proxying - any latency numbers?

[08:24] Priya: slight overhead for mTLS (10-30ms) depending on handshake and cipher suites. with session resumption it's negligible. proxying through egress proxies introduces RTT but we tune keepalives and connection pooling to reduce per request latency. we can run a specific benchmark during pilot.

[08:42] James: Network segmentation - can we host different LOBs in separate clusters/namespaces for tenant separation?

[08:50] Priya: yes - we support multi-tenant isolation per cluster, dedicated node pools per tenant, and namespaced RBAC. you can also pin tenants to dedicated GPU pools for stronger isolation.

[09:02] Marcus: for on-prem air-gapped installs, what's the update and patch process? we have strict change windows.

[09:10] Priya: we provide signed update artifacts and offline installer bundles. patching is a planned activity: you'll receive a release with checksums and a remediation plan; our SE will assist with patch windows. you can opt out of automatic updates.

[09:26] Samantha: evidence for ISO27001: we need policy mapping and statement of applicability. do you provide that?

[09:32] Liam: yes, we provide ISO27001 control mappings and SoA artifacts to customers under NDA. we'll attach the mapping and our certified scopes.

[09:43] James: last one - egress monitoring: can we set alerts for anomalous egress patterns?

[09:48] Priya: yes, logs can be piped to your SIEM and you can run rules against bytes per minute, unusual IP destinations, DNS spikes, etc. we also emit metrics for unusual model usage.

[10:00] Martin: ok wrapping - quick recap, we'll send SOC2 + ISO artifacts, Priya will share network and firewall examples and ALB config, Marcus will send VPC details. next step pilot onboarding week of 6/15. any other blockers?

[10:13] Marcus: none from my side, maybe just procurement questions that Samantha will raise later.

[10:20] Samantha: i'll review the audit bundles when you send them. thanks.

[10:26] Martin: thanks everyone. we'll follow up via email with the artifacts and a calendar invite for the onboarding.

-- End of transcript (transcription contains occasional recognition errors and minor speaker attribution issues).
